title: About the author
body: This website is written by Mohd Elfie Nieshaem Juferi, an apologist writing from the Islamic side of the question of the Injīl: what the Qur’an means by the Gospel it affirms, what the four gospels are, and how the two stand to each other. The writer’s other work, including the case against Paul of Tarsus at apostleofdoom.org, is reached through menj.org.
## How the website is written

Every page states which of three positions it takes: the scholarly consensus, a minority view within scholarship, or the Islamic position argued by the writer. The labels are on the page, at the top, so that a reader is never left to guess whether a sentence is reporting what historians agree on or what the writer believes. Where the Islamic position differs from the consensus, as on the crucifixion, the page says so in plain words and does not pretend the consensus is weaker than it is. Sources are listed at the foot of each article, and the works most used are gathered in the source library.

The rule that decides what gospel material the website keeps is stated once, on the measure, and applied everywhere. The Gospel According to Islam that the website carries is Ahmad Shafaat’s, and how it was composed is set out step by step. Errors, when found, are corrected on the page and recorded in the corrections log with what the page said and what it says now.
## What the website is not

It is not a work of academic scholarship, though it depends on one and cites it. It is not neutral; it argues a case, and it says so. It is not a polemic against Christians, who are addressed throughout as readers to be persuaded by evidence they can check. The writer asks of the Christian reader what Shafaat asked in 1985: to read a Muslim gospel as one would read a book from a church other than one’s own, and to judge it by its sources.
## Getting in touch
To report an error, propose a source or disagree with a reading, see the contact page. Replies that improve a page are acknowledged in the corrections log.

title: Terms of use
body: These terms govern the use of injil.help. They are short because the website is simple: it offers text for study and asks only for fair dealing in return.
## The text

The text of this website is offered for study and discussion. You may quote it, at reasonable length, with credit to injil.help and a link to the page quoted. You may not republish whole articles, or the gospel sections, without permission; ask through the contact page, and permission is normally given for non-commercial use with credit.

The text of The Gospel According to Islam, sections 1 to 27 and the Introduction, is by Ahmad Shafaat (Vantage Press, 1985), and the Qur’anic passages are in The Clear Quran translation by Dr. Mustafa Khattab; their reuse is governed by their own rights holders. See the credits page.
## Images and icons

Manuscript images are loaded from Wikimedia Commons under the licence named in each caption, most of them public domain; those licences govern their reuse, and the Kairouan Qur’an photograph (Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0) must keep its credit. The share icons are from the Minimalist Social Icons Pack (GPL); the LinkedIn icon is by Font Awesome under CC BY 4.0. The brand marks remain the trademarks of their owners and are used only to link to those networks’ own sharing pages.
## Links and sharing

The share links under each page open the sharing page of the network you choose, in a new tab, on that network’s own website, with the page address and title filled in. Nothing is posted without your action there, and this website does not see what you share. Links to other websites are given for reference; this website is not responsible for their content.
## Accuracy

The content is offered in good faith, states which position it takes on each page, cites its sources, and is corrected when errors are found; the corrections log is the record. It is not legal, medical or professional advice, and it is not the teaching of any institution. Nothing on this website should be taken as the last word on a question of history or faith; the sources are given so that readers may go to them.
## Conduct

Correspondence must be civil. Abuse is not answered and will be removed from any public record. Disagreement, however firm, is welcome, and the best of it is published and answered on Objections and replies.
## Changes
These terms may change as the website does. The date of the last change is the date of the most recent entry in the corrections log that names this page.

title: Privacy policy
excerpt: What this website collects and what loads from other sites.
body: This website collects as little as a website can. This page says what that is, what loads from other servers when you read a page, and what happens when you use the share links.
## What this website collects

This website runs on WordPress. WordPress sets cookies for people who log in to the administration area and for people who leave a comment; the theme does not enable comments, so for a reader neither applies. The theme itself sets no cookies and loads no analytics, no advertising and no tracking script of any kind. The fonts are served from this website, not from Google or any other font service. The web server keeps the ordinary access logs that every web server keeps (the address requested, the time, your browser’s identification and IP address); they are used to keep the site running and are not analysed for anything else.
## What loads from other websites

Manuscript images load from Wikimedia Commons (upload.wikimedia.org). When a page with such an image opens, your browser contacts Wikimedia’s servers to fetch it, and Wikimedia can see your IP address and the page that referred you, under its own privacy policy. No other third-party content is loaded on any page of this website: the pattern, icons, share icons and the default social image are all served from here.
## Share links

Under each page there is a row of share links. Each is an ordinary link to the sharing page of a network (X, Facebook, WhatsApp, Telegram, Reddit, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Threads, Pinterest or LINE), which opens in a new tab on that network’s own website with the page address and title filled in. No script from any of those networks runs on this website, no network is told that you visited a page unless you click its link, and nothing is shared until you confirm it on the network’s own page, under that network’s privacy policy. The “Copy link” button copies the page address to your clipboard and sends nothing anywhere. The “More…” button, where your browser shows it, opens your device’s own share sheet; what happens after that is between you and your device.
## Contact

If you write to the author through the contact details on the contact page, your message is used to reply to you and is not shared with anyone or added to any list. A correction you report may be acknowledged in the corrections log; your name is not published there unless you ask.
## Your rights
Since no personal data is collected or stored beyond server logs and any message you choose to send, there is nothing to export or delete except that message, which will be deleted on request.
## Changes
If analytics, a comment system, an email service or any other third-party service is added, this page will be updated to name it before it goes live, and the change will be logged.

title: Contact
body: The writer can be reached through menj.org. There is no comment form on this website, by design; correspondence is answered directly.
## Reporting an error
Every page of this website is open to correction, and the corrections log records each one in public. A report is most useful when it gives:
- the address of the page and the sentence in question;
- what you believe is wrong, and the source that shows it (chapter and verse, manuscript, or a scholarly work with a page number);
- if the point is one of reading rather than fact, the alternative reading and who holds it.
A report that turns out to be right is corrected on the page and logged with the date, what the page said and what it now says. A report that is not accepted receives a reply saying why.
## Proposing a source or a reading

The source library lists the works the website relies on. Suggestions of works that bear on a page, from any side of the question, are welcome, and so are Christian replies to the arguments made here; the strongest of them are set out and answered on Objections and replies and Responses to named articles, and that is where a well-made reply will end up.
## Reuse and sharing

Pages may be quoted with credit and a link, and every page carries share links under its text; see the terms of use for republication. Questions about the Qur’anic text, the translation used, or the credits for the gospel are answered on the credits page.

title: Credits
excerpt: Sources and credits for the texts, images and design of injil.help.
body: ## Texts

- The Gospel According to Islam, sections 1 to 27 and the Introduction: Dr. Ahmad Shafaat, The Gospel According to Islam (New York: Vantage Press, 1985). Spelling and scanning errors were corrected. The text and notes follow the arrangement of The Narrative of Jesus, Son of Mary, in which the Qur’anic passages are set among the sections and the notes are numbered through the whole.

- The Gospel According to Islam, printed edition: Mohd Elfie Nieshaem Juferi, The Gospel According to Islam (Seri Kembangan: Langgam Fikir, first edition, 2028). The text on this website was checked against the book.

- The Qur’anic passages on Jesus, with their headings and footnotes: Alham Ahmed, The Gospel According to the Quran: Jesus and His Teachings (Toronto: Noor Lal Foundation, 2021), in the translation The Clear Quran by Dr. Mustafa Khattab (Al-Furqaan Foundation, theclearquran.org), which the compiler acknowledges using with the foundation’s permission.
- An Epistle unto the Congregation of Paul of Tarsus: an English rendering of the Malay letter Epistel Kepada Jemaat Paulus, with footnotes added by this website.

- The Gospel of Thomas: sayings are numbered as in the standard edition. The summaries woven into the gospel are this website’s own, prepared from Thomas O. Lambdin’s translation in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988), and checked against the two translations printed in full on their own pages: Mark M. Mattison’s, based on Nag Hammadi Codex II, 2, which its translator has placed in the public domain (gospels.net, a Luminescence, L.L.C. website; the manuscript dates follow the same site), and Stephen Patterson and Marvin Meyer’s, from The Complete Gospels: Annotated Scholars Version, ed. Robert J. Miller (Polebridge Press, 1992, 1994), reproduced with permission. The introduction’s dating, manuscripts and the debate over independence draw on Peter Kirby, Early Christian Writings (earlychristianwritings.com/thomas.html), who cites Ron Cameron, Stephen Patterson and Stevan Davies.

- The witnesses to the substitution, at section 26: paraphrases of Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4, on Basilides; of the Second Treatise of the Great Seth (Nag Hammadi Codex VII, 2), after Roger A. Bullard and Joseph A. Gibbons; and of the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter (Codex VII, 3), after James Brashler and Roger A. Bullard, both in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988). In each the laughter attributed to Jesus, and in the two Nag Hammadi texts their docetism and their polemics, are set aside and the notes say so. On the lost gospel: Bart D. Ehrman, “The Lost Gospel of Basilides”, The Bart Ehrman Blog, 1 July 2023.

- The classical commentaries on the Qur’anic passages about Jesus (al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Tanwīr al-Miqbās, al-Jalālayn, al-Durr al-Manthūr and al-Saʿdī): English renderings prepared for this website from the public-domain Arabic texts published at tafsir.app and, for Tanwīr al-Miqbās, at shamela.ws (book 12877); the modern editors’ apparatus is not translated. The renderings are released with the site and may be quoted with credit and a link; they have not been checked by a second translator, and the Arabic source is named on every page.

- The Islamic Dilemma, answered: the sections on the origin of the argument, its four substitutions, the Bible’s textual history, Paul, the four registers of the verses and the added questions draw on the study Reconsidering the “Islamic Dilemma” by Mohd Elfie Nieshaem Juferi (Kuala Lumpur, 2026), with the scholarship it cites named on the page.

- Thomas and the synoptic gospels: the sayings-order test: the analysis, tables and quotations come from the note “Correlation Analysis”; it draws on Helmut Koester’s list of parallels, R. McL. Wilson (1960) and Stephen Patterson (1988). The page restates it in this website’s words.

- The infancy gospels, Q and the manuscript table: the summaries are this website’s own, prepared from Mark M. Mattison’s public-domain translations of the Infancy Gospel of James and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, from his edition of Q (based on The Critical Edition of Q), and from the manuscript information, all at gospels.net.
- All other text, including the section titles, the colour-coded Gospel of Thomas sections and their notes, the answers and the replies: this website.
## Images
Manuscript images load from Wikimedia Commons. Each carries its credit and a link to its Commons page in its caption.
## Design
Built on the Twenty Twenty-Five theme. Typefaces keep their own licences; see the licence files in the theme’s font folder.

The ornament of this website, the eight-pointed star lattice behind every page, the dividers and the stylised icons, follows a principle rather than a fashion. Al-Fārūqī argued that the Muslim artist’s stylisation of the natural figure, and his final turn to pure geometry and to a pattern that repeats without end, are the visual form of lā ilāha illā Allāh: a refusal to let anything in nature stand for the divine, and an attempt to express not God, who cannot be expressed, but His inexpressibility, by setting the eye on a course it cannot complete. The lattice here is drawn in that spirit. Nothing on the site figures the divine; the only images are manuscripts, which are the evidence. See Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (1983), pp. 28-32.
Share icons are from the Minimalist Social Icons Pack (GPL). The LinkedIn icon is by Font Awesome, CC BY 4.0.
